profile.summary: Proverbs is a collection of practical wisdom for daily life, offering instructions, alerts and discernment for concrete decisions. His focus is not only to teach good advice, but to form character: to act prudently in the crisis, patience under pressure, meekness in the face of challenges and firmness against temptation. The book insists that true wisdom begins with a reverent relationship with God and that without this spiritual basis, even the best counsel loses its center. Although it gathers sayings of various times and contexts, the book was shaped to guide the reader in real situations of life, from family and work to social coexistence and conduct before authorities.
profile.setting: Proverbs gathers wise sayings from various periods and social contexts of ancient Israel. Many proverbs fit into the real court environment, especially when dealing with behavior before kings and authorities. Others appear in a family and rural scenario, and there are also sayings related to commerce, work and business. Tradition attributes the beginning of the collection to Solomon, but the final form of the book seems to have been consolidated centuries later, with additions and organization by other scholars and editors, such as the counselors of Hezekiah, Agur, Lemuel and groups identified only as "the wise." The work was directed mainly to young people in formation, but their reach is broader and worth it for any reader.

structure.label: Initial paternal speeches
structure.description: First major section of the book, marked by continuous instructions of a father to his son, with calls to listen, warnings against foolish paths and appeal to the search for wisdom.

structure.label: Collections of proverbs and wise sayings
structure.description: Second large section, formed by a broad anthology of short proverbs, observations and warnings about wealth and poverty, planning, laziness, work, relationships, pride, humility and other themes of common life.

themes: True wisdom begins in the fear of the Lord and not just in life technique.
Biblical wisdom is practical: it guides concrete decisions, moral choices and daily coexistence.
The book counterposes the path of the sage and the path of the fool, showing general consequences of each posture.
Character matters as much as the result: prudence, humility, diligence and self-control appear as marks of wise life.
Proverbs express generally true but not automatic promises for every situation.
readingKeys: Read by observing poetic parallels: many lines repeat, contrast or complete the previous idea.
Notice the context of each proverb before applying it; some advice is worth in certain situations and not in others.
Notice that the book forms a spiritual call, not only moral: the source of wisdom is the right relationship with God.
profile.cautions: Proverbs should not be read as a book of absolute and mechanical promises. His sayings present widely true principles, but do not guarantee the same result in all circumstances; wise reading requires discernment of context. The authorship and final composition are complex questions: the tradition links the book to Solomon, but the collection includes materials from other sages and editors, and its final form seems later than the Solomonic era. It should also be noted that many proverbs were originally directed to a young, especially masculine audience, but the book is, in the whole, to all readers.

dossier.narratedEra: Main setting in ancient monarchic Israel, especially in royal court contexts, home/family, agriculture and trade. The notes also place some proverbs in relations with neighboring peoples of the ancient Near East, especially Egypt and possibly the region of Mass in Proverbs 30-31. The book presents everyday life situations that can cross various epochs of Israel, but the narrative and social frame evoked is that of a pre-exile and monarchic Israeli society.
dossier.compositionEra: The composition is presented in the notes as a collection of sayings of different times and social contexts, initiated by Solomon and completed/edited by other wise and compilers later. The notes mention additions and final edition several centuries after Solomon, with collections associated with the officers of Hezekiah in Proverbs 25:1, in addition to Agur and Lemuel in Proverbs 30-31. The final form is therefore post-salomonic, although Solomon is the main authority and traditional starting point.

politics.title: Solomon as Israel's king-wise and authority
politics.detail: The notes describe Solomon as a very wise king, of great wealth and broad rule, who ruled over all of Israel and used his wisdom to guide others. He is the main author/penman of Proverbs in the tradition of notes.
politics.readingImpact: The reading of the book gains courteous and state weight: many sayings are not abstractions, but advice for decisions of government, discipline and administration of life under real authority.

politics.title: Real cut as a frequent scenario of proverbs
politics.detail: The introduction states that many proverbs have as their primary scenario the royal court, dealing with how to act before a king. In Proverbs 16:10-15, the series is explicitly read as reflection on the king, representative of God's power on earth.
politics.readingImpact: This guides the reader to listen to various proverbs as instructions of political and social prudence, not only as private morals; honor, favor and control of speech before power become central themes.

politics.title: Hezekiah and the later collection of proverbs from Solomon
politics.detail: The notes say that about two hundred years after Solomon, the servants of Hezekiah of Judah gathered additional proverbs from Solomon and added them to anthology.
politics.readingImpact: The reader realizes that the work has an editorial history and that the salomonic collection was preserved, selected and transmitted in a later monarchical environment, which helps to explain the internal variety of the book.

politics.title: Other names associated with the sapiential tradition: Agur and Lemuel
politics.detail: The notes identify Agur (30:1) and Lemuel (31:1) as other composers or editors mentioned in Proverbs. In 31:1-9, Lemuel is treated as an unknown figure outside of this text; the notes suggest that he, like Agur, could be Mass.
politics.readingImpact: This prevents reading Proverbs as a homogeneous work of a single author. The presence of distinct names broadens the political-cultural horizon of the book and shows that its wisdom circulated in different leadership circles.

politics.title: Just governance and defense of defense of the defenseless
politics.detail: Proverbs 31:8-9 presents the king as one who should speak for the helpless, while 16:12-15 associates the government with righteousness and the wise use of power. The notes suggest that the ideal king needs divine wisdom and self-control.
politics.readingImpact: The text is read as criticism and guidance for the exercise of power: royalty is not mere privilege, but ethical responsibility before God and the vulnerable.

customs.title: Instruction of father and mother to young son
customs.detail: Chapters 1-9 are described as a father-to-child discourse, with occasional mention of the mother. The notes understand this as a family environment of moral formation; the reception may have been for a biological child or, according to the aforementioned debate, an apprentice.
customs.readingImpact: The reader should listen to much of Proverbs as domestic pedagogy, not just as a collection of loose maxims. This explains the pastoral, repetitive and disciplinary tone of warnings.

customs.title: Training for a profession and practical learning
customs.detail: The introduction says that many exhortations adjust to a young man starting a profession; the material deals with occupation, diligence and the way of life. The comparison with the Instruction of Amenemope also suggests a context of sapiential school education.
customs.readingImpact: Proverbs can be read as an initiation manual for adulthood and work. Advice on choices, diligence and relationships are not theories, but training for everyday life.

customs.title: Economy, trade and business
customs.detail: The notes claim that part of the book belongs to the world of commerce, exchange and business. In 31:16-18, the virtuous woman participates in commercial ventures; in 31:13-15 and 31:22-24, she administers food supply, clothing and family reputation.
customs.readingImpact: The reader sees that biblical wisdom achieves concrete economic activity, not just abstract worship or morals. The productive work appears as a virtue and family responsibility.

customs.title: Table, food and drink as signs of self-control
customs.detail: In 31:4-7, the king is warned against the excess of wine, for he must keep the senses alert; Lemuel is instructed by his mother not to waste energy with alcoholism and disorderly desires.
customs.readingImpact: This shows that meals and drink were a relevant part of social and political life, and that the book uses them as a test of moral sobriety and leadership ability.

customs.title: Domestic life, house provision and honor
customs.detail: Proverbs 31:13-15 and 31:22-29 describe a house managed with work, clothing, food, benevolence and public reputation. The note about the virtuous wife emphasizes activity inside and outside the home.
customs.readingImpact: Reading starts to value the house as an economic and active moral unit, not just private space. The excellence of women impacts the honor of the husband and community.

customs.title: Poverty, generosity and care for the vulnerable
customs.detail: The notes highlight frequent contrasts between wealth and poverty and, in 31:19-21 and 22-23, the generosity of the virtuous woman and the opening to the poor. In 16:16, wealth is relativized before wisdom.
customs.readingImpact: The reader is led to realize that economic status is not the ultimate end of wisdom; the generous use of goods and the protection of the weak are part of just life.

language.title: Hebrew parallelism and poetic form
language.detail: The notes explain that Proverbs is compact Hebrew poetry, with synonymous, antithetical and comparative parallelism. Examples cited include 16:13, 14:1 and 15:16.
language.readingImpact: The interpretation should pay attention to the relationship between the two members of the verse, because the meaning arises from contrast, reinforcement or comparison. This prevents fragmented readings of each line in isolation.

language.title: Proverb as a riddle, observation and rule of life
language.detail: The introduction defines proverbs as socially recognized short sayings that express observation, advice or practical truth. In 1:6, the aforementioned Hebrew word is explained as "enigmas" or "paradoxos" that require interpretation.
language.readingImpact: The reader should expect conciseness and flexibility of application. Proverbs does not function as a mechanical manual, but as wisdom that needs to be discerned according to the situation.

language.title: Personification of Wisdom as a woman
language.detail: The notes note that wisdom is personified as a woman in 1:20-33, because it is the feminine Hebrew noun. In 3:18 and 8:1-9:6 this develops into a figure that invites the listeners.
language.readingImpact: The personification intensifies the appeal of the book: choosing wisdom is to respond to a living voice, not just accept a rule. This also connects to the child's call to "embrace" wisdom.

language.title: Language of the two paths
language.detail: The notes in 1:8-19 speak of two ways in the book: a wise and just, another fool and evil. This image organizes prologue and moral choice.
language.readingImpact: The reader understands that many exhortations of Proverbs function as road bifurcations: follow the instruction of parents or enter the path of violence, greed and self-destruction.

language.title: Images of ornament, crown and honor
language.detail: In 1:9, 3:22 and 16:31, wisdom appears associated with crown, chain of honor, and gray hair as glory. Notes treat these images as reward and dignity.
language.readingImpact: Reading gains an aesthetic and symbolic dimension: wisdom is not only usefulness, but moral beauty that adorns life and confers social honor.

language.title: Language of domination, government and moral authority
language.detail: Matthew Henry notes that the term for proverb has the idea of governing or exercising dominion, because of the force of wise sentences. The 16:10-15 notes also highlight the royal function of divine wisdom.
language.readingImpact: This suggests that the book wants to shape the reader through short sentences with authority, almost like compact moral laws, able to govern consciousness.

timeline.title: Wisdom of Solomonic in its traditional origin
timeline.detail: The notes link Proverbs to Solomon, especially to his request for wisdom and the use he made of it to rule and teach. The exact date is not given, but the framework is the psalomonic reign.
timeline.readingImpact: The reader understands that the tradition of the book is born at the height of the Israeli monarchy and carries real prestige from the beginning.

timeline.title: Proverbs 22:17-24:22 and possible ancient Egyptian influence
timeline.detail: The introduction states that the "trinta" of the wise men seem to have taken much of The Instruction of Amenemope, an Egyptian work around 1100 BC.
timeline.readingImpact: This extends the reading to an international sapiential dialogue. The book of Proverbs appears as an Israeli tradition that dialogues with materials from the ancient Near East without losing its theological identity.

timeline.title: Collection of the officers of Hezekiah, about two centuries after Solomon
timeline.detail: The note of 25:1 places a second editorial stage long after Solomon, when officers of Hezekiah collected additional proverbs from Solomon.
timeline.readingImpact: The collection should not be read as a frozen document; its preservation by scribes and wise men in later times shows continuous use and selective review.

timeline.title: Acrescimos of Agur and Lemuel in the final section
timeline.detail: The notes identify Agur in 30:1 and Lemuel in 31:1 as names linked to the last sections of the book, with no more firm historical information beyond the text itself.
timeline.readingImpact: The end of Proverbs preserves non-salomonic voices, remembering that biblical wisdom was gathered over time and not by a single hand.

timeline.title: Final edition several centuries after Solomon
timeline.detail: The introduction states that Proverbs reached its final form several centuries after Solomon. Matthew Henry also organizes the book as a set with preamble, Solomon's collections and diverse final sections.
timeline.readingImpact: The reading must respect the final form of the book, without erasing its compositional history. The reader finds theological unity, but also real editorial layers.

investigation: The confessional tradition presented attributes the beginning of the work to Solomon, but the notes also recognize later collection and different editors; this requires distinguishing traditional authorship of final arrangement.
The possible relationship with Amenemope is presented as strong similarity, not as a proven dependence independently.
The identification of Mass for Agur and possibly Lemuel is only suggested in the notes of 31:1; there is no broader historical confirmation in the sources provided.
Some details about the school and professional context of Proverbs 1-9 are inferences of grades, not direct historical statements.
Matthew Henry's notes bring broad devotional and theological observations; they were used only when explicitly linked to the book and not as external historical proof.
dossier.limits: The dossier depends solely on the notes provided and therefore only reflects what they claim or suggest. There are real gaps on exact dating, location of authors such as Agur and Lemuel, and on the historical extent of Egyptian influence. The coverage is selective: it privileges themes explicitly discussed in the introductory notes and in Proverbs 1, 16 and 31. Some points are interpretations of the grades themselves, especially when they speak of a professional environment, the final editorial section or the possible school use of the proverbs. No external historical data, no speculative chronologies, nor reconstructions of events outside the available textual support were added.
